name: Convertible crib
tagline: Two ends, two sides, a mattress support, and eight barrel nuts that fight you. The build is easy. Getting it right is what matters.
peopleNote: One person can do it. A second pair of hands makes holding a side upright much easier.

standard.name: ASTM F1169 / 16 CFR 1219
standard.note: Full-size cribs sold in the US must meet 16 CFR 1219. As of 1 August 2026 the mandatory version is ASTM F1169-25. Your manual prints the version it was built to — older cribs commonly say F1169-10a. A crib built to a 2010 revision is still legal to own and use, but if you are buying second-hand, that date is worth knowing.

tools.why: Usually an M4. It is the only wrench the crib needs.
Not supplied, and not optional. You use it to rotate the barrel nuts so the bolt can find the thread. Without it this job is miserable.
Looking down bolt holes to see which way a barrel nut is facing.

tools.n: A soft blanket or the flattened box
tools.why: You will lay crib ends on their face. Cribs are usually the nicest finish in the room.

provided: Long bolts for the sides (often M6 x 60mm)
Shorter bolts for the mattress support (often M6 x 18mm)
Mattress support with a warning pouch attached
before: Do not use a power screwdriver or a drill on a crib. Manufacturers say this explicitly. Power tools strip the wood thread and snap bolts, and a stripped crib bolt is not a cosmetic problem.
Build it in the nursery. An assembled crib does not fit through a standard doorway.
Count every bolt and barrel nut against the parts list before you start. Crib makers ship missing hardware free and fast, but only if you find out on day one.
Keep the instruction booklet. There is a pouch sewn to the mattress support specifically to store it, because you will need it again when you convert the crib.
safety: Never substitute hardware. A hardware-store bolt that looks identical is not grade-matched to a crib bolt, and crib hardware is engineered for repeated impact loading. Order the real part.

Tighten every fastener fully. CPSC testing found that a crib fastener backed off as little as half a turn loses its clamping force, and side-impact loading then works it looser. The gap that opens up is an entrapment and strangulation risk.
No pillows, comforters, bumpers or extra padding go in the crib. Padded crib bumpers are banned in the US under the Safe Sleep for Babies Act.
Stop using the crib when your child reaches 35 inches tall, or starts climbing out — whichever comes first.
Never place a crib near a window, or anywhere a blind or curtain cord can reach it.

steps.title: Check for a recall before you build it
steps.say: Two minutes, before any tools come out. Cribs are recalled more than almost any furniture, and a recalled crib is not something you want to discover after assembly.
do: Find the model and lot number on the label, usually on the bottom rail of a crib end
Search that model at cpsc.gov/recalls
Register the crib with the manufacturer so they can reach you if one is issued later
steps.tip: Registration is the only way a manufacturer can warn you. It takes a minute and they do not use it for marketing.
steps.watch: This matters most for a hand-me-down or second-hand crib, where no registration card ever reached you and the original box is long gone.

steps.title: Lay everything out and count it
steps.say: Four big parts and three kinds of hardware. Lay them out, match them to the parts page, and count the bolts and barrel nuts before anything else.
do: Left end, right end, two sides, and the mattress support
Long bolts for the sides, short bolts for the mattress support — they are not interchangeable
Barrel nuts: small metal cylinders with a threaded hole through the middle
steps.tip: Check the pre-assembled parts too. Manuals say to confirm that factory-assembled joints are tight, and sometimes they are not.
steps.watch: If anything is missing or damaged, stop and call the manufacturer. Do not improvise with hardware from a drawer.

steps.title: Understand the barrel nut — this is the whole job
steps.say: A barrel nut is a metal cylinder that drops into a round hole in the crib end, with a threaded hole running across it. The bolt comes in from the side and has to thread into that cross hole. If the barrel nut is rotated even slightly, the bolt cannot find it.
do: Drop the barrel nut into its hole
Look at the slot on its end — that slot tells you which way the threaded hole is pointing
Turn the slot with a flat-head screwdriver until the threaded hole lines up with where the bolt will come from
Hold it there with the screwdriver while you start the bolt by hand
steps.tip: Sight down the bolt hole with a flashlight. You should be able to see straight through the barrel nut's threaded hole. If you see metal, rotate it.
steps.watch: This single step is where nearly everyone gets stuck and starts to believe the parts are faulty. They almost never are. The barrel nut is just facing the wrong way.

steps.title: Attach the first side to both ends
steps.say: Stand the two ends up and bring one side between them. Start all four bolts by hand before tightening any of them. The frame needs slack to find its shape.
do: Both ends upright, side panel between them
Barrel nuts rotated and held with the screwdriver
Every bolt started by hand, several turns, before the wrench touches anything
steps.tip: Lean the ends against a wall or a box so they stay upright while you work. Or have someone hold them.
steps.watch: If a bolt will not start with finger pressure, do not force it with the wrench. You are cross-threading, and the thread you are destroying is in the barrel nut.

steps.title: Fit the mattress support — springs up, pouch up
steps.say: The mattress support drops in and bolts at all four corners. It has an orientation: the springs face up, and the warning pouch sewn to it must face up too.
do: Springs facing up, pouch facing up
One bolt in each of the four corners
Tighten all four with the Allen wrench
steps.tip: The pouch facing up is not cosmetic. It is where the instructions live, and the warnings printed on it have to stay readable for the life of the crib.
steps.watch: These four bolts are the single most important fasteners in the crib, and they are also the ones you will never see again once the mattress goes in. Mattress support failures — loose pins, broken brackets — are the most repeated structural recall in this entire product category.

steps.title: Choose the mattress height now
steps.say: Most cribs have three positions. Highest is only for a newborn who cannot push up. Drop it as soon as your baby can sit, and drop it again before they can stand.
do: Highest position: newborn only, while they cannot push up on their own
Middle: once they can sit up unaided
Lowest: before they can pull to standing — not after
steps.tip: Moving the support later means undoing four bolts. It is a ten-minute job, so do not put it off.
steps.watch: With the mattress at its highest setting, the top of the crib side must sit at least 3 inches above the mattress surface. If it does not, you are already one position too high.

steps.title: Attach the second side
steps.say: Same as the first: barrel nuts rotated, all four bolts started by hand, then tightened. The crib becomes rigid as soon as this side goes on.
do: Rotate each barrel nut and hold it with the screwdriver
All four bolts hand-started first
Then tighten
steps.tip: If the holes do not quite line up, loosen the bolts on the opposite side a turn or two. The frame will shuffle into place.

steps.title: Tighten properly — and know what tight means
steps.say: Go around every bolt and bring it up firm, then do a second lap. Firm means the wrench stops turning easily and the joint has no movement. Not gorilla-tight, because you are pulling steel into wood.
do: Short end of the Allen wrench in the bolt, long end in your hand, for more control and less force
Tighten until the resistance climbs sharply, then stop
Second full lap, because tightening one bolt loosens its neighbor
Grab the top rail and try to rack the crib — there should be no movement and no creak
steps.tip: If a bolt keeps turning without ever firming up, the barrel nut is spinning in its hole or the thread has stripped. Stop and get a replacement part.
steps.watch: Never finish a crib with any fastener less than fully seated. Half a turn of slack is enough to let impact loading open a gap.

steps.title: The two-finger mattress gap test
steps.say: Put the mattress in and push it tight to one side. If you can fit more than two fingers between the mattress and the crib frame at any point, the mattress is too small for this crib.
do: Press the mattress firmly into one corner
Try to slide two fingers into the gap on the opposite side and at both ends
More than two fingers of gap means the wrong mattress, not a crib to work around
steps.tip: A full-size crib mattress is a regulated size: at least 51 5/8 inches long and 27 1/4 inches wide, and no more than 6 inches thick. Buy to that spec and the gap takes care of itself.
steps.watch: Mattress fit is the most recalled failure in this category — undersized mattresses, mattresses sold for the wrong frame, extra padding added on top. A gap at the side of a crib is where infants become trapped. No crib manual we reviewed actually tells you to run this test.

steps.title: Check the slats and the rail height
steps.say: Slats must be no more than two and three-eighths inches apart — about the width of a soda can. None should be loose, cracked, or missing.
do: Try to pass a standard soda can between any two slats: it should not fit
Push each slat and check for movement
Confirm no cracks, especially where slats meet the rails
steps.tip: Slat spacing is set at the factory, so this is really a check for shipping damage and for second-hand cribs that have been apart and back together.
steps.watch: Wider slat spacing has triggered real recalls. If a can passes through, stop using the crib and contact the manufacturer.

steps.title: Set the re-check reminder before you walk away
steps.say: Every crib manual says to inspect periodically and none of them tell you how often. Put it in your phone now: monthly, and after any move.
do: Monthly recurring reminder, two minutes each time
Also after any house move, any disassembly, and whenever the mattress height changes
steps.tip: The schedule in the next section tells you exactly what to check each time, and it takes less time than making the bed.

recheck.what: Grab the top rails and rack the crib side to side. Any movement or creak means a bolt has backed off. Go around all twelve with the Allen wrench.
Reach under the mattress and check the four mattress-support bolts. These are the ones you cannot see, and they are the most common structural failure in cribs.
Run the two-finger gap test again. Mattresses compress and shift, and babies grow into the gap.
Run a hand down every slat looking for cracks or movement, especially where the slat meets the rail.
Full re-tighten of every fastener. Wood threads lose grip a little each time a crib comes apart, so a crib on its third assembly needs more attention, not less.

recheck.when: Each time you lower the mattress
recheck.what: You already have the wrench out and four bolts undone — re-tighten everything else while you are there.
Re-check the model number at cpsc.gov/recalls. Recalls get issued years after a crib ships.

fixes.q: The bolt will not go into the barrel nut
fixes.a: The barrel nut is rotated the wrong way. Put a flat-head screwdriver in the slot on its end and turn it until you can see daylight through its threaded hole when you sight down the bolt hole. Hold it there while you hand-start the bolt. This is the answer about nine times out of ten.

fixes.q: The barrel nut keeps falling out of its hole
fixes.a: Hold the crib end flat so the hole faces up and gravity keeps the nut seated, or put a small piece of tape over the outside of the hole while you start the bolt. Some people use a magnetic screwdriver to hold it in position.

fixes.q: A bolt spins forever and never tightens
fixes.a: Either the barrel nut is rotating in its hole, or the thread has stripped. Try holding the barrel nut still with the screwdriver. If it still spins, stop and order a replacement barrel nut — do not leave that joint partly tight.

fixes.q: The frame is twisted and rocks on the floor
fixes.a: Loosen every bolt a couple of turns, stand the crib on a flat floor, press down on each corner so it settles square, then re-tighten in two laps. Tightening a crib while it sits on carpet or an uneven floor locks the twist in.
Check the pouch sewn to the mattress support — that is what it is for. Otherwise every major manufacturer has manuals by model number on their site, free.

fixes.q: I am missing a bolt and the store is closed
fixes.a: Wait. Do not substitute. Crib bolts are specified for repeated impact loading and a visually identical hardware-store bolt is not the same part. Every manufacturer ships crib hardware free, usually within a few days.

fixes.q: The crib creaks when the baby moves
fixes.a: A creak is a joint moving. Do a full two-lap re-tighten including the four mattress-support bolts underneath. If it still creaks, find which joint by rocking the crib with a hand on each joint in turn.

fixes.q: It is a hand-me-down and I do not know its history
fixes.a: Check the model against the CPSC recall list, confirm no drop-side (those have been banned since 2011), run the soda-can slat test and the two-finger mattress test, and fully re-tighten every fastener. If any hardware is missing, order it new from the manufacturer rather than using the crib as-is.
